title: Does studying longer mean higher quiz scores?
subtitle: Follow Maya Chen, a fictional first-year PhD student, through her first small observational study.
disclosure: Teaching simulation: all people, source excerpts, conversations, reviews and data are invented. Numerical results were computed by the app’s real R runner when this demo was built. Opening the demo makes no AI calls and runs no analysis.

stages.title: Explore a research interest
stages.where: Discuss this step with your guide → Write and explain your decisions → Supervisor checkpoint
stages.input: Maya starts with an interest in study habits and an eight-row synthetic class dataset.
turns: Maya · researcher
I want to prove that more studying improves learning. Can you write my question?
Methods mentor · simulated agent
Let’s begin with the problem and why it matters. We do not need a final research question yet. What interests you, and what do you need to learn from existing research?
Maya · researcher
I’m interested in study habits and learning. A possible teaching dataset has self-reported hours and quiz scores, but I need to understand what those measures can establish.
Methods mentor · simulated agent

Study habits and learning give us a preliminary direction. In the literature review, examine how studies measure learning, what theories they use and what confounding they address before settling on a question.
Maya · researcher

I accept an initial research direction, not a final question. I will read about study time, prior achievement and learning measures, then refine an answerable question. I still need to justify the scope and contribution.
stages.artifact:
Initial research direction: Study habits and learning in a fictional university class.
Motivation: Understand how students study and how their learning is assessed.
Tentative interest: Whether time spent studying relates to learning outcomes.
Reading priorities: Key concepts, possible mechanisms, outcome definitions, selection and alternative explanations.
Possible access: Synthetic records are available for the tutorial; a real project would need access and permissions.
Open decisions: The refined question, scope, literature contribution and design will follow reading. No novel gap or causal conclusion is claimed.
stages.understanding: This direction is a starting point. The literature may change my concepts, scope and question; supervisor feedback here does not freeze them.
stages.review: Fictional supervisor: The initial direction is suitable for exploratory reading. A final question, confirmed dataset and research gap are not required at this checkpoint.
stages.carry: Carry the motivation and open questions into the literature review. Return to this direction if the reading changes the scope.

challenge.question: What should this first step establish?
choices: A final question and a proven research gap before reading
An initial direction and the questions the literature review should explore
challenge.feedback: Agree a useful direction first. Reading then helps refine the question and assess whether a contribution is defensible.

stages.title: Review literature and refine the question
stages.where: Inspect sources and save passages → Check claims against source passages → Write and explain your decisions
stages.input: The initial direction is study habits and learning. Reading helps define concepts, examine explanations and refine the question; this is existing literature, not results from the new study.
turns: Maya · researcher
I found an example passage saying students who study more score higher. Can I cite it as proof that studying works?
Evidence mentor · simulated agent
Inspect the exact passage and its design. Link a narrow claim to the source and record evidence that challenges your expectation.
Maya · researcher
Teaching source S1 reports an association, but no random assignment. S2 says that accounting for prior achievement weakened the association. Both are fictional teaching excerpts, not publications.
Evidence checker · simulated agent
S1 supports a reported association in its sample. It does not establish causation or support a claim about every student. S2 motivates confounding as a design limitation.
Maya · researcher
I reject my causal claim. I record a narrower claim and mark its support as limited to the quoted teaching passage. A real project needs verified papers and a documented search.
Maya · researcher

After considering those concepts and limitations, I refine my question: In this synthetic class sample, how are weekly self-reported study hours associated with quiz scores? This tiny synthetic exercise illustrates methods, not a verified new contribution to the literature.

sources.title: Teaching excerpt A — unadjusted study-time association (fictional)
sources.passage: In this fictional observational class sample, students reporting more weekly study hours tended to have higher quiz scores. Study time was not randomly assigned.
sources.limitation: No causal identification; narrow setting; self-reported exposure.

sources.title: Teaching excerpt B — prior achievement matters (fictional)
sources.passage: In this fictional example, the association between study time and quiz performance weakened after prior achievement was included in the model.
sources.limitation: Illustrates a competing explanation; it is not real empirical evidence.

stages.artifact:
Search plan for real work: Search appropriate scholarly databases for (study time OR study hours) AND (quiz OR academic performance) AND university; record database, date, query and inclusion decisions. No real search was performed in this demo.
S1: A fictional unadjusted association; inspected passage does not justify causation.
S2: A fictional example challenging the simple story through prior-achievement adjustment.
Claim C1: S1 describes an association in its fictional sample. Decision: Accept this narrow reading only.
Rejected claim: S1 proves study hours improve learning.
Gap: This exercise explores a small dataset; it establishes no novel literature gap.
Conceptual framing: Study time is a possible correlate of performance; prior achievement and motivation are rival explanations. A single quiz does not represent all learning.
Refined research question: In this synthetic class sample, how are weekly self-reported study hours associated with quiz scores?
Objective: Describe an unadjusted association with uncertainty, without making a causal claim.
Contribution: A worked teaching example only; no verified literature gap or empirical novelty.
Hypotheses: No confirmatory hypothesis test or preregistration is claimed.
Refinement: Narrowed a broad practical interest to measured variables in one synthetic sample.
stages.understanding: Reading changed a broad interest into a bounded question by clarifying concepts, measurements and alternative explanations. Real work would need verified literature and a defensible contribution.
stages.review: Fictional supervisor: The evidence logic is adequate for a tutorial. These excerpts cannot be cited in a real manuscript; conduct and verify a real literature search. The checkpoint now considers the explicit refined question, concepts and feasibility; it does not certify a novel gap from invented sources.
stages.carry: The explicit refined question and conceptual limitations now guide the study protocol. If further reading changes them, revise this step and renew affected downstream reviews.

challenge.question: Which question matches the available design?
choices: Does extra studying cause better learning?
How are recorded study hours associated with quiz scores?
challenge.feedback: The second question matches an observational comparison. Writing a causal question does not make the data causal.

stages.title: Plan the study and methods
stages.where: Discuss this step with your guide → Write and explain your decisions → Supervisor checkpoint
stages.input: The saved question asks for an association; the evidence map identifies prior achievement as a possible confounder.
turns: Maya · researcher
Which analysis will give the most significant result?
Methods mentor · simulated agent
Choose the analysis from the question before inspecting the estimate. What is the observational unit, missing-data rule and scope of the model?
Maya · researcher
One row is one fictional student. I will fit quiz_score ~ study_hours using rows with both values. I will report how many rows are excluded.
Methods mentor · simulated agent

That is a simple unadjusted regression supported by this app. Check linearity, residual patterns and influential observations. The small sample makes these checks weak; no prior-achievement variable is available.
Maya · researcher
I accept that limitation and freeze the plan. This is an authored teaching sequence, not a timestamped preregistration. A real analysis must disclose prior exposure to results.
stages.artifact:
Design: Small observational secondary analysis of synthetic records. Unit: One fictional student per row.
Model: quiz_score = intercept + slope × study_hours + error.
Primary quantity: Unadjusted slope in quiz points per additional reported study hour, with a model-based 95% confidence interval.
Missing data: Complete cases on the two selected variables; report total, included and excluded rows. No imputation.
Diagnostics: Inspect fitted values and residuals; assess linearity and unequal variance cautiously. Influence and sensitivity analyses require further work.
Assumptions: Independent observations, an adequate linear conditional mean, and model assumptions for interval estimation.
Confounding: Prior achievement and motivation are unmeasured; no causal interpretation.
Prior exposure: Authored synthetic tutorial, constructed with known results; not preregistered research.
Ethics: No real people; real studies require institution-specific ethics and data-access checks.
stages.understanding: Selecting a method to obtain a small p-value would change the question after seeing the answer. Missingness can also select a biased subset.
stages.review: Fictional supervisor: Approve this limited teaching protocol. Do not present eight invented observations as a powered study or preregistration.
stages.carry: The exact variables, complete-case rule and noncausal interpretation guide profiling, execution approval and consistency checks.

stages.title: Obtain and prepare the data
stages.where: Data / Analysis tasks → Import a permitted CSV dataset → Write and explain your decisions
stages.input: The protocol specifies two numeric variables and complete-case analysis. In this example the data are already available synthetic records; new data collection would take place outside the app after the relevant permissions and protocol decisions.
turns: Maya · researcher
I have uploaded the synthetic CSV. Should I replace blanks with zero?
Data mentor · simulated agent
No. A missing quiz is not a zero quiz score. Inspect missingness, units, ranges and provenance before running the planned analysis.
Maya · researcher
There are eight records, one missing study-hours value and one missing quiz score on different rows. Six rows have both variables. Recorded hours range from 1 to 7; recorded scores from 2 to 12.
Data mentor · simulated agent
Keep the original CSV and its hash. Report why two rows are excluded and what is unknown about missingness. A numeric profile alone cannot establish that each row is a unique eligible person.
Maya · researcher
The tutorial author defines each row as a distinct fictional student. I retain NA and blank cells, use the planned six complete cases, and document that no missingness mechanism is known.
stages.artifact:
Dataset D1: synthetic-study-hours.csv; eight author-created rows, two numeric columns.
Dictionary: study_hours = weekly hours, nonnegative; quiz_score = points, 0–15.
Observed ranges: Hours 1–7; quiz scores 2–12. No recorded out-of-range value.
Missingness: Row 7 has no quiz score; row 8 has no study-hours value. Six complete cases; two excluded from regression.
Identity: Exact CSV preserved and SHA-256 recorded with the execution bundle.
Duplicates and eligibility: All rows are distinct by tutorial construction; no real participant identity verification was performed.
Cleaning: No value replacement or imputation.
Protocol deviations: None. Unknown missingness mechanism limits interpretation.
stages.understanding: Replacing a blank with zero would invent a measurement and change the slope. Exclusion counts alone do not prove missingness is harmless.
stages.review: Fictional supervisor: The missing-data decision matches the protocol. Retain the original rows and report the reduced analysis sample.
stages.carry: The dataset hash and variable mappings bind the approved plan to the exact input used in R.

challenge.question: How many rows should the planned regression use?
choices: All 8, replacing missing values with zero
challenge.feedback: Six rows match the planned complete-case rule. Zero replacement would invent data and deviate from the protocol.

stages.title: Approve the plan and inspect real outputs
stages.where: Data / Analysis tasks → Propose a plan → Review script → Approve → Run
stages.input: The saved question, design and data report constrain the plan. The dataset has six complete cases.
turns: Maya · researcher
Please propose the analysis using my saved protocol and dataset profile.
Analysis mentor · simulated agent
Use the fixed simple linear regression template: outcome quiz_score, predictor study_hours. Omit incomplete rows as planned. This estimates an unadjusted association.
Maya · researcher
I review the variable mapping, complete-case rule and exact R script. I approve this plan for these synthetic data and run it.
Local R runner · recorded computation
The attached execution record contains the actual numerical outputs from the app’s R template, including coefficients, confidence intervals, residuals, counts and session information.
Maya · researcher

Six rows were used and two excluded. The slope is about 1.943 quiz points per hour, with a model-based 95% interval of 1.568 to 2.318. The residuals are small in this constructed dataset, but six observations cannot establish that the assumptions hold.
Analysis mentor · simulated agent
Keep the code, input and outputs together. If the question, design or data report changes, review a new current plan before rerunning; an old output cannot silently answer a revised question.

Execution: R1, computed from synthetic data using the app’s fixed local R template.
Model: quiz_score ~ study_hours, six complete cases from eight rows.
Slope: 1.942857 quiz points/hour; model-based 95% CI 1.567972 to 2.317742.
Intercept: -0.133333 quiz points.
Reproduction: Save input.csv and analysis.R from the bundle in a clean directory, then run Rscript analysis.R. Exact versions are in session.txt.
Diagnostics: Inspect diagnostics.csv. The exact fitted values and residuals are in the attached output; estimates may be sensitive to individual rows. No comprehensive influence or sensitivity assessment was performed.

stages.understanding: The language model proposed a plan; R computed the numbers. Approval records a deliberate decision, not proof that the chosen model is scientifically adequate.
stages.review: Fictional supervisor: The run is reproducible. Keep the limitations visible and do not mistake a narrow model interval for reliable evidence about real students.
stages.carry: Recorded estimates and exclusions feed the claims and consistency review. The original input, exact script and environment accompany the research package.

stages.title: Interpret findings in context
stages.where: Write and explain your decisions → Consistency review → Researcher response
stages.input: The question and protocol are noncausal. R1 estimates an unadjusted slope from six synthetic complete cases.
turns: Maya · researcher
My conclusion is: Each extra hour of study improves students’ quiz scores by 1.94 points.
Consistency reviewer · simulated agent
Mismatch: the protocol says “no causal interpretation,” but “improves” implies causation. The output is an unadjusted association in six synthetic records.
Maya · researcher
I accept that finding. I revise the claim: In six complete synthetic records, one additional reported study hour was associated with an estimated 1.94-point higher quiz score.
Critical reviewer · simulated agent
Add uncertainty and plausible alternatives. Prior achievement, motivation and selective missingness remain unresolved. The fictional sources do not independently validate the result.
Maya · researcher

I save the corrected interpretation and rerun the consistency review so it checks the current version. The scripted follow-up finds no remaining causal wording mismatch; that is not a certification of quality.
stages.artifact:
Claim linked to R1: In six complete synthetic records, one additional reported study hour was associated with an estimated 1.94-point higher quiz score (model-based 95% CI 1.57–2.32).
Rejected wording: “Each extra hour improves scores.”
Alternative explanations: Prior achievement, motivation, reporting error and missingness.
Limits: Tiny constructed sample; no confounder adjustment; no causal identification or external generalizability.
Consistency response: Accepted the causal-language finding and revised the artifact. A new scripted review checks the revised version; the previous review remains historical.
Unknown: Whether a similar association exists in a real population or changing study time causes any benefit.
stages.understanding: A fitted slope does not show what an intervention would do. A consistency check can detect contradictions but cannot supply missing data or validate the study.
stages.review: Fictional supervisor: The revised wording matches the design and output. It remains a demonstration, not an empirical finding for publication.
stages.carry: The corrected claim, uncertainty, competing explanations and unresolved limitations must all remain in the final manuscript.

challenge.question: Does a clean consistency review establish that this study is rigorous?
choices: Yes; all scientific problems are resolved
No; aligned claims still need sound data, methods and expert review
challenge.feedback: Consistency is one check. It cannot establish source truth, adequate power, valid assumptions or freedom from bias.

stages.artifact:
TEACHING REPORT — synthetic data; no real empirical claims
Title: Study hours and quiz scores in a fictional class: a reproducible demonstration.
Question: How are weekly study hours associated with quiz scores in this synthetic sample?
Methods: Eight constructed records; unadjusted simple linear regression; six complete cases, two excluded. No imputation. No preregistration or real literature search.
Results: Estimated slope 1.94 quiz points/hour (model-based 95% CI 1.57–2.32). The exact computation, input and environment are attached.
Discussion: This illustrates workflow continuity and reproducibility. The result establishes nothing about real students and cannot support an intervention recommendation.
Limitations: Invented sources and observations; tiny sample; missingness; unmeasured confounding; incomplete diagnostic assessment.
Transparency: Conversations and reviews are authored simulations. Numerical outputs come from actual local R execution. All teaching materials are labeled fictional.
Package: Walkthrough and decision record, two teaching excerpts, original CSV, selected R input, fixed script, coefficients, diagnostics, figure, log and session information.
Next real-world step: Develop an adequate study with verified literature and expert supervision.
stages.understanding: A complete package lets another person inspect what I did and why. Reproducibility is necessary, but does not make a weak or fictional study valid.
stages.review: Fictional supervisor: Teaching walkthrough complete. No real supervisor approval, ethics approval or publication readiness is implied.
stages.carry: Download the materials below, then return to your notebook. To practice execution, import the synthetic CSV under Run analysis and review your own plan before running it.

overview: Maya starts with a practical interest, reads teaching excerpts to clarify concepts and refine a question, plans a study, prepares synthetic data, reviews an R analysis, interprets its limits and assembles a report. The walkthrough shows a suggested route; real research involves revisiting earlier decisions.

dataset.name: synthetic-study-hours.csv
dataset.permission: Author-created fictional observations for a public teaching demonstration; no real participants.

plan.rationale: Estimate the unadjusted association between study hours and quiz scores in synthetic records. Omit incomplete cases; no causal interpretation or confounder adjustment.
plan.script:
# ResearchGuide analysis template v1; input.csv uses y (outcome) and optional x (predictor).
# Complete-case analysis: blank/NA values are excluded and counts are recorded.
options(warn=1)
d <- read.csv('input.csv', na.strings='NA', check.names=FALSE)
original_n <- nrow(d)
d <- d[complete.cases(d), , drop=FALSE]
if (nrow(d) < 3) stop('Too few complete observations.')
write.csv(data.frame(total=original_n, used=nrow(d), excluded=original_n-nrow(d)), 'counts.csv', row.names=FALSE)
describe <- function(v) c(n=length(v), mean=mean(v), sd=sd(v), median=median(v), min=min(v), max=max(v))
write.csv(data.frame(variable=names(d), t(vapply(d,describe,numeric(6))), check.names=FALSE), 'descriptives.csv', row.names=FALSE)
if (length(unique(d$x)) < 2 || length(unique(d$y)) < 2) stop('Regression requires variation in both variables.')
fit <- lm(y ~ x, data=d)
if (fit$rank < 2) stop('The regression design is rank deficient.')
sm <- summary(fit)
ci <- confint(fit,level=0.95)
write.csv(data.frame(term=rownames(sm$coefficients), estimate=sm$coefficients[,1], std_error=sm$coefficients[,2], statistic=sm$coefficients[,3], p_value=sm$coefficients[,4], lower_95=ci[,1], upper_95=ci[,2]), 'coefficients.csv', row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(data.frame(n=nrow(d), r_squared=sm$r.squared, residual_sd=sm$sigma, residual_df=df.residual(fit)), 'fit.csv', row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(data.frame(fitted=fitted(fit), residual=residuals(fit)), 'diagnostics.csv', row.names=FALSE)
print(sm)
print(ci)

# A reproducible SVG histogram generated from R-computed bin counts.
h <- hist(d$y, plot=FALSE)
height <- 240; width <- 480
bars <- vapply(seq_along(h$counts), function(i) {
 bh <- if(max(h$counts)>0) h$counts[i]/max(h$counts)*180 else 0
 sprintf('<rect x="%.2f" y="%.2f" width="%.2f" height="%.2f" fill="#214f42"/>', 40+(i-1)*400/length(h$counts), 200-bh, 390/length(h$counts),bh)
}, character(1))
svg <- paste0('<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 480 240"><rect width="480" height="240" fill="#f7f5ed"/><text x="40" y="20">Outcome distribution (complete cases)</text>',paste(bars,collapse=''),sprintf('<text x="40" y="225">Range: %.4g to %.4g; n = %d</text>',min(d$y),max(d$y),nrow(d)),'</svg>')
writeLines(svg,'figure.svg')
write.csv(data.frame(lower=head(h$breaks,-1), upper=tail(h$breaks,-1), count=h$counts),'histogram.csv',row.names=FALSE)
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()),'session.txt')
print(data.frame(total=original_n,used=nrow(d),excluded=original_n-nrow(d)))
